prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The wind blew high, the waters raved, A ship drove on the land, A hundred human creatures saved Kneel’d down upon the sand. Three-score were drown’d, three-score were thrown Upon the black rocks wild, And thus among them, left alone, They found one helpless child. A seaman rough, to shipwreck bred, Stood out from all the rest, And gently laid the lonely head Upon his honest breast. And travelling o’er the desert wide It was a solemn joy, To see them, ever side by side, The sailor and the boy. In famine, sickness, hunger, thirst, The two were still but one, Until the strong man droop’d the first And felt his labours done. Then to a trusty friend he spake, “Across the desert wide, O take this poor boy for my sake!” And kiss’d the child and died. Toiling along in weary plight Through heavy jungle, mire, These two came later every night To warm them at the fire. Until the captain said one day, “O seaman good and kind, To save thyself now come away, And leave the boy behind!” The child was slumbering near the blaze: “O captain, let him rest Until it sinks, when God’s own ways Shall teach us what is best!” They watch’d the whiten’d ashy heap, They touch’d the child in vain; They did not leave him there asleep, He never woke again.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, Kneel, Three

outputs.L1:
The wind blew high, the waters raved;  
A ship drove on the land.  
A hundred human creatures, saved,  
Knelt down upon the sand.

Three-score were drowned, three-score were thrown  
Upon the black rocks wild;  
And thus, among them, left alone,  
They found one helpless child.

A seaman rough, to shipwreck bred,  
Stood out from all the rest,  
And gently laid the lonely head  
Upon his honest breast.

And, travelling o’er the desert wide,  
It was a solemn joy  
To see them ever side by side—  
The sailor and the boy.

In famine, sickness, hunger, thirst,  
The two were still but one,  
Until the strong man drooped the first  
And felt his labours done.

Then to a trusty friend he spoke:  
“Across the desert wide,  
O take this poor boy for my sake!”  
He kissed the child and died.

Toiling along in weary plight  
Through heavy jungle mire,  
These two came later every night  
To warm themselves beside the fire.

Until the captain said one day,  
“O seaman, good and kind,  
To save thyself, now come away  
And leave the boy behind!”

The child was slumbering near the blaze:  
“O captain, let him rest  
Until it sinks, when God’s own ways  
Shall teach us what is best!”

They watched the whitened, ashen heap;  
They touched the child in vain.  
They did not leave him there asleep—  
He never woke again.
outputs.L2:
A fierce wind whipped the sea into a fury and forced a vessel ashore. One hundred survivors fell to their knees on the beach. Sixty people had drowned, while another sixty had been hurled against the dark, jagged rocks. Amid the wreckage, they discovered a single defenseless child with no one beside him.

One hardened sailor, long familiar with shipwrecks, stepped forward from the crowd. With tenderness, he drew the orphaned child’s head against his sturdy chest. As the company crossed the vast desert, the sight of the sailor and the boy always together brought a grave kind of happiness.

Through famine, illness, hunger, and thirst, the man and child remained inseparable. At last, however, the powerful sailor was the first to weaken, knowing that his struggles had reached their end. He called upon a dependable companion and begged him to carry the unfortunate boy across the great desert for his sake. Then he kissed the child and died.

The trusted man and the boy continued onward, struggling through dense jungle and deep mud. Each night they reached the fire and warmed themselves beside it. One day, the captain urged the kind sailor to abandon the child and escape while he still could.

The boy lay sleeping close to the flames. The sailor asked the captain to let him remain undisturbed until the fire had burned down, trusting that God’s will would then show them what to do. They waited until only a pale mound of ashes remained and tried unsuccessfully to rouse the child. They did not desert him while he slept—for he never opened his eyes again.
outputs.L3:
A violent shipwreck drove the vessel onto the shore. The impact spared about one hundred people, but many others were lost to the sea or hurled to their deaths upon the rocks.

Among the survivors was a rough seaman who discovered a helpless child amid the confusion. Moved by compassion, he took the boy into his care and became his protector. From that moment on, the two were rarely apart. Together they endured hunger and thirst, sickness and exhaustion, as well as the terrible hardships of a long journey across the desert.

At last, the sailor grew too weak to continue. Realizing that he was dying, he entrusted the child to a faithful friend and begged him to watch over the boy. Soon afterward, the seaman died, leaving the child to travel on without the man who had saved and cared for him.

The survivors pressed forward through dense jungle and deep mire, but the journey had already taken too great a toll. One night, utterly exhausted, the child lay down beside the fire and fell asleep. By morning, the others discovered that he had quietly died in the night and would never wake again.
outputs.L4:
The poem recounts a tragic story of shipwreck, endurance, and selfless devotion. After a vessel is destroyed at sea, a sailor survives the disaster only to find himself stranded in a barren desert. Amid the wreckage and loss, he discovers an orphaned child and resolves to protect him. Although the sailor is exhausted, injured, and tormented by thirst, he carries the child onward, placing the boy’s safety above his own. Their struggle through the desolate landscape becomes a test not only of physical endurance but also of compassion in the face of almost certain death.

Realizing that he will not survive, the sailor entrusts the child to a faithful companion. His final concern is not for himself but for the orphan, whom he hopes may still be saved. The companion accepts this responsibility and continues the desperate journey, caring for the child with the same tenderness and loyalty. Yet their courage cannot overcome the merciless conditions surrounding them. Despite every sacrifice made on his behalf, the child eventually dies.

The poem’s conclusion emphasizes the cruelty of fate and the limits of human effort. Neither bravery nor devotion can prevent the final loss, but the sailors’ actions are not rendered meaningless. Their willingness to protect the helpless, honor one another’s trust, and remain loyal amid extreme suffering reveals their moral strength. Through the deaths of the sailor and the child, the poem presents a deeply moving vision of compassion that persists even when hope has vanished.
outputs.L5:
### The Three Who Kneel

At the edge of the silent kingdom stood three travelers: a warrior, a scholar, and a child. Before them rose an ancient stone carved with the words:

**“The strongest kneel not from weakness, but from wisdom.”**

The warrior knelt to honor those he had failed to protect.  
The scholar knelt to admit how little she truly knew.  
The child knelt to plant a single seed in the barren earth.

Years later, armies had vanished, books had turned to dust, and the travelers were forgotten. Yet from that seed grew a vast tree beneath which all people could find shelter.

Of the three who chose to kneel, it was the smallest who changed the world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a traditional English ballad about a shipwrecked sailor who rescues an orphaned boy and carries him across a desert.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Ballad of the Salt-Sea Man**

The *Mary Anne* went down by night  
Beneath a crooked moon;  
The waves they rang like iron bells,  
The storm-wind cried her doom.  

Of thirty souls that sailed aboard,  
But one came to the strand—  
Old Thomas Grey, with bloodied brow,  
Upon the desert sand.  

He heard amid the broken spars  
A cry both frail and wild;  
And in a chest, by mercy spared,  
He found a little child.  

“Where bide thy folk, my bonny boy?  
Where may thy mother be?”  
“They sleep,” he said, “beneath the foam,  
And will not wake for me.”  

Then Thomas bound the boy to him  
With canvas, cord, and band:  
“Though Death may rule the rolling deep,  
He shall not rule the land.”  

**O bitter blew the salt-sea wind,  
And white the hot sun shone;  
The sailor bore the orphan boy,  
And crossed the waste alone.**  

For seven days no rain-cloud rose,  
No green thing blessed their sight;  
The sand burned red beneath the noon  
And froze beneath the night.  

He gave the child the water first,  
And took the lesser share;  
He shaded him with tattered sail  
When fire was in the air.  

“O set me down,” the small boy wept,  
“Your strength is near its end.”  
“I’ve borne,” said Grey, “the ocean’s wrath;  
I’ll bear my captain’s friend.”  

On the ninth morn his knees gave way  
Beside a dry ravine;  
Then far away a palm-tree stirred,  
A little thread of green.  

He raised the lad upon his back,  
Though dim his old eyes grew,  
And staggered toward that distant shade  
As seamen steer by blue.  

**O bitter blew the salt-sea wind,  
And white the hot sun shone;  
The sailor bore the orphan boy,  
And crossed the waste alone.**  

At dusk they reached a shepherd’s well,  
Where cool the water ran;  
The child was lifted safe and sound—  
But silent lay the man.  

They buried Grey beneath the palms,  
Far from the English foam;  
The boy grew tall and crossed the seas  
To seek the sailor’s home.  

And there he told by winter fire  
How Thomas kept his word;  
The old wives wept, the young men bowed,  
And every sailor heard.  

Now when a ship rides through the storm,  
Or lost men cross the sand,  
They sing of Grey, who conquered both  
With one child in his hand.  

**O bitter blow the salt-sea winds,  
And fierce the desert sun;  
But love may cross the loneliest waste  
When hope and strength are done.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a tragic narrative poem in rhyming quatrains about survivors of a maritime disaster, focusing on the bond between a rugged seaman and a helpless child.
counterfactuals.output:
The midnight sea broke black with foam,  
The mast was split, the lantern drowned;  
A handful watched their burning home  
Sink with a long and hollow sound.  

Among them crouched old Marlow Dane,  
A rope-scarred hand, a storm-gray eye;  
He bore the salt of forty rains  
And knew how quietly men die.  

Beside him, in the shattered boat,  
A child lay weak with cold and fright;  
He wrapped her in his tattered coat  
And held her through the starless night.  

“Your name?” he asked. She whispered, “May.”  
He said, “Then May must meet the morn.”  
Though wind and hunger gnawed away,  
He smiled as if the dawn were born.  

The others drank the meager rain  
And watched the empty waters roll;  
But Marlow sang an old refrain  
To keep the terror from her soul.  

For seven days the sun burned white;  
For seven nights the cold winds cried.  
He gave her every crumb by night  
And kept no morsel at his side.  

At last a distant sail appeared,  
A pale wing on the golden foam;  
The weary survivors wept and cheered—  
But Marlow knew he’d not reach home.  

He raised the child with failing hands  
So those aboard might see her there;  
Then slipped beneath the rescue bands,  
Still smiling through his salt-stiff hair.  

They drew May safe against the rail;  
She called his name across the blue.  
No answering voice rose through the gale—  
Only the gulls that wheeled and flew.  

And years thereafter, by the shore,  
She lit one lamp when storms began;  
Its beam swept out forevermore  
To find the lost, rough-hearted man.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a Wordsworth-style poem in archaic language where a sailor saves a boy after a shipwreck, entrusts him to a friend, and the child later dies beside a campfire.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Mariner’s Charge**

Beneath a wan and winter moon,  
When winds did vex the deep,  
A shattered bark went drifting by  
Like some dread thing in sleep.  

The billows brake upon her ribs,  
The mast was rent in twain;  
And through the dark a seaman heard  
A child’s voice o’er the main.  

“Ho! little one, take fast mine hand!”  
The hardy sailor cried;  
He plunged amid the whitening foam  
And drew him from the tide.  

The boy was pale, his raiment torn,  
His locks with sea-brine wet;  
Yet round the seaman’s neck he clung,  
As ivy clingeth yet.  

Three days they wandered o’er the strand,  
Where neither hearth nor hall  
Gave token through the misty waste,  
Nor answer to their call.  

At length beside a forest road  
They met an ancient friend,  
A keeper of the mountain sheep,  
Right faithful to the end.  

“Good Edrick, take this orphaned child;  
Be thou his roof and stay.  
For I must seek the distant port  
Ere dawn hath kindled day.  

“I saved him from the cruel flood,  
But cannot bide him near;  
Then love him for the dead men’s sake,  
And keep him from all fear.”  

The shepherd laid his hand in his:  
“By bread, by salt, by stone,  
This tender waif shall share my fire,  
Nor ever dwell alone.”  

So forth the mariner strode apace,  
Nor once behind him gazed;  
And long his darkling figure showed  
Where frosty hill-paths raised.  

But ere the spring had loosed the brook,  
Or lark resumed her song,  
A fever seized the rescued boy  
And held him all night long.  

Beside the fire he lowly lay,  
Wrapped in a mantle brown;  
The red flames climbed the ashen brands,  
Then softly fluttered down.  

“O tell the man who fought the sea,”  
The child in faintness said,  
“I dreamed his hand was over me,  
And stars were overhead.  

“And tell him that I feared no wave,  
Nor wind upon the wild;  
For once he bore me through the storm  
As fathers bear a child.”  

The shepherd bent above his face;  
The fire sank dim and low.  
Outside, amid the solemn pines,  
There fell a soundless snow.  

At morn the embers all were white,  
The little heart was still;  
And day arose with golden feet  
Beyond the lonely hill.  

Full many a year the sailor came  
Unto that woodland place,  
And sat beside the cold hearthstone  
Where last had shone that face.  

He spake no word, but through the trees  
The wandering breezes stirred;  
And in their mournful, tender breath  
A child’s farewell was heard.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Tell a sorrowful story in verse about courage, sacrifice, and companionship during a perilous journey through desert and jungle.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn we crossed the copper waste,  
three shadows walking west—  
Mara with her father’s blade,  
Tarin with a wounded chest,  
and I, who bore the water skin  
and swore we all would rest.

The desert raised its burning walls;  
the sky withheld its rain.  
Our footprints vanished one by one  
beneath the wind’s red mane.  
Yet when I fell, they carried me  
and sang against the pain.

On the seventh night the water failed  
beneath a starless dome.  
Tarin gave his final share  
and spoke of fields at home.  
“Drink,” he said, “for one must live  
to tell how far we’d come.”

At morning, raiders found our trail—  
black spears against the sun.  
Mara turned and drew her blade  
while Tarin bade me run.  
Two stood fast where three had walked,  
and bought the life of one.

I reached the jungle’s emerald gate  
with grief beside me still.  
The vines hung thick as mourning cloth,  
the rivers sought to kill.  
At night I heard my comrades’ songs  
in every bird and rill.

Deep beneath the dripping leaves  
I found the shrine we sought:  
a stone that marked the hidden spring  
for which our homes had fought.  
I broke the seal; the waters rose—  
but joy returned me not.

I carried back the river’s course  
through roots and burning sand.  
It filled the wells, it fed the wheat,  
it greened the wounded land.  
The children danced where Mara fell  
and drank from Tarin’s hand.

Now every year I journey west  
when desert roses bloom.  
I lay three cups beside the dunes,  
though two remain in gloom.  
For courage is the road we take,  
and love—who shares the doom.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write an old-fashioned lyrical ballad beginning with a violent storm and ending with shipwreck survivors discovering that a sleeping child has died?
counterfactuals.output:
The thunder brake on Carrick Head,  
The foam flew white as bone;  
The black gale smote the shuddering mast,  
And made the deep to moan.  

The lightning rent the midnight clouds  
And showed the leaping sea;  
“Lord Christ,” the grey-haired skipper cried,  
“Have mercy now on me!”  

The mainmast bowed, the mainmast burst,  
The sails went whirling wide;  
Three times the ship rose like a bird,  
Then groaned upon her side.  

The women clung unto the rails,  
The men to spar and rope;  
While through the roar a mother sang  
A little hymn of hope.  

She wrapped her child within her cloak  
And held him to her breast:  
“Sleep sound, my lamb, though wild winds rave;  
The dawn shall bring us rest.”  

But down there came a mountain wave,  
Green-walled and crowned with white;  
It swept the mother from the deck  
And quenched the lantern-light.  

At morn the storm had spent its wrath;  
The gulls wheeled low and cried,  
And seven souls on splintered planks  
Were borne against the tide.  

They gained at last a barren strand  
Beneath a leaden sky;  
No hearth was there, no shepherd’s cot,  
No sail went passing by.  

Among the wrack of mast and chest,  
Half-buried in the sand,  
They spied the mother’s tattered cloak  
Still knotted by her hand.  

Within it lay the little child,  
As peaceful as in bed;  
They whispered, “Wake—the storm is gone,”  
But found the sleeper dead.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
